extracted.intended_audience: journalism educators, composition instructors, and researchers in writing assessment
extracted.subtask_description: Evaluating the effect of including a unit of basic news writing in English Composition I on students' writing performance and attitudes (measured pre/post across several affective and skill dimensions).

rubrics_metrics.name: Anxiety toward writing (Geer Fear Survey)
rubrics_metrics.description: Anxiety measured by responses to the Geer Fear Survey (Geer, 1965) with educationally-induced stimuli added (Raisman, 1984). The survey lists fear-producing stimuli; this study used items such as 'failing a test,' 'writing papers for a grade,' 'teachers,' 'English classes,' 'spelling words,' and 'reading.' Students rate each item on a scale of 0 (no reaction) to 6 (terror).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used as the main hypothesis measure. For analysis the author grouped/totaled responses; in one analysis the three items 'writing papers for a grade,' 'English classes,' and 'spelling words' were summed and compared pre/post between groups using t-tests. Interpretation: lower post-test scores indicate reduced anxiety.

rubrics_metrics.name: Self-assessment of writing ability (questionnaire)
rubrics_metrics.description: Students' self-rating of their own writing ability measured via a questionnaire designed for the study; Questionnaire A and B each contained seven items intended to measure self-assessment on a 5-point Likert scale (5 = usually 'excellent' or 'very', 1 = 'poor' or 'not at all').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Change in each student's rating from pre-test to post-test was analyzed (chi square on rating-change frequencies). No single item among the seven showed a significant relationship with treatment in this study.

rubrics_metrics.name: Attitude toward writing (questionnaire)
rubrics_metrics.description: Students' attitudinal responses about writing measured via three items on the study's questionnaire (Questionnaires A and B used identical attitude items), rated on a 5-point Likert scale.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Chi square tests compared frequency distributions of rating changes pre/post between treatment and control groups. In this study none of the attitude items showed a statistically significant treatment effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Motivation to improve writing (questionnaire)
rubrics_metrics.description: Motivation measured via four items on the custom questionnaire, using a 5-point Likert response format to capture students' motivation to learn and improve writing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analysis employed chi square on pre/post rating changes; none of the four motivation items indicated a significant relationship with the news-writing treatment in this sample/semester.

rubrics_metrics.name: Perceived practicality of instruction for work after college (questionnaire)
rubrics_metrics.description: Students' view of how practical/helpful the composition instruction would be for the world of work, measured by three items on Questionnaire B; key item wording: 'How helpful for the world of work do you view the writing instruction you received in English Composition I this fall?' (5 = very to 1 = not at all).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Chi square analysis found a statistically significant relationship between the treatment and students' perceptions of practicality (chi square = 13.197, p = 0.010), i.e., treatment students viewed instruction as more practical for work after college.

rubrics_metrics.name: Grammar and mechanics skills (English 3200 pre/post test)
rubrics_metrics.description: Objective measurement of grammar and mechanics using the English 3200 pre-test and post-test from the Joseph Blumenthal programmed usage text (100-point test).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Improvement measured as the difference between post-test and pre-test scores and compared across groups using the t-test. In this study mean improvements (control = 4.46, treatment = 5.33) were not significantly different (p = 0.7363).

rubrics_metrics.name: Writing skills — holistic essay scoring
rubrics_metrics.description: Writing performance assessed by a writing exercise given pre- and post-study; two instructors evaluated each student's response using a holistic grading scale (average of two raters used).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Inter-rater correlation reported (.84). Improvement computed as post-test minus pre-test average holistic score and compared between groups via t-test. In this study treatment improvement (.7500) was greater than control (.5263) but not statistically significant (p = 0.3296).

rubrics_metrics.name: News writing content / production criteria
rubrics_metrics.description: The study's operational definition of 'news writing content' included instruction in the basic form and style of news writing: 'the inverted pyramid, lead writing, short paragraphs, attribution to source material, use of third person, and an emphasis on conciseness and brevity.' The approach emphasized less personal/subjective writing and less creativity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These are the specific production features taught in the treatment (one-half semester). They serve as criteria when evaluating students' produced news writing (e.g., presence of a clear lead, appropriate attribution, concise sentences, correct third-person voice, logical inverted-pyramid structure).

rubrics_metrics.name: Diversity of instructional content (exposure to multiple forms/styles)
rubrics_metrics.description: Pedagogical desideratum that composition instruction expose students to a 'full range of compositional possibilities' (Weathers) and 'other equally valid forms of clothing' (Perelman) — i.e., include varied/ interdisciplinary approaches such as news, business, technical, and referential writing alongside traditional essay forms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used as an evaluative criterion for course design: courses that include multiple discourse modes (referential/news, persuasive, literary, expressive) better prepare students for diverse real-world writing tasks. The paper argues for measuring effects of such diversity, ideally with longer/longitudinal studies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Realistic audience and use of body of knowledge
rubrics_metrics.description: Criterion that student writing be oriented to a realistic audience and, when appropriate, be grounded in a body of knowledge (e.g., interviews, fact sheets) rather than produced ex nihilo as purely expressive writing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The literature and argument suggest assignments that create immediate/real audiences (e.g., journalistic contexts) improve engagement and higher-order skills. As an evaluative dimension, presence of a defined audience and use of external sources/content is desirable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clarity and conciseness as quality markers
rubrics_metrics.description: Preference for clear, simple, and concise prose (characteristic of journalistic writing) over ornate, wordy prose; cited authorities: 'the most common reason for bad writing... Most writers have just never learned how to write clearly' (Williams) and Mencher's claim that journalistic writing is clear and simple.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating student writing, favor metrics/criteria that reward directness, economy of language, and clarity of expression. Be aware of anti-patterns noted in literature: graders with English backgrounds may prefer wordy/muddy prose; explicit training and rubrics should counteract that bias.

rubrics_metrics.name: Holistic grading procedures and rater reliability
rubrics_metrics.description: Use of a holistic grading scale for essay evaluation with multiple raters; the study reports a rater correlation of .84 on initial placement essay scoring.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practices: have two raters score each essay, average scores for analysis, and report inter-rater reliability. Holistic scoring is suitable for pre/post comparisons of general writing quality, but may mask specific skill gains unless complemented by objective tests (e.g., grammar/mechanics exam).
